attributes.title: Level 4

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you reorder the sequence of colors in the palette to make the seasonal shades easier to locate?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Which colors are missing from the default Arcade color palette?

❓ What colors might be useful for 4 seasonal background images?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that there are 4 different ways to select a new color. In the Color Palette editor, the ninja can enter the 6-digit hex color code to select a specific color. This is helpful if they already know the hex color codes for a specific palette they would like to use. The ninja can also click on the color box where there are 3 additional options for selecting a specific color: the sliders, the eyedropper tool, or RGB values. If using the sliders, point out that the upper slide adjusts the color hue while the lower slider adjusts the color. If using the eyedropper tool, the ninja can hover it over any pixel on screen, even on a different tab or window, to select that pixel color. If using the RGB values, they will need to use a number 0-255 for each of the 3 values to create a different color.

💡Remind the Ninja that Player image assets will be used in this project, so they may not want to change the colors that are used widely in person sprites.

💡Alternatively, the Ninja may use one of the preset color palettes from the dropdown menu.
steps.instructions:
Start the project by customizing the Assets menu color palette!


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen. On the left side menu, click on the Colors button. Notice the colors in the default Arcade color palette.


In this project, 4 image assets will be customized to showcase the 4 seasons. Think about what alternative colors might be useful to include in the color palette to customize the sky, grass, and/or leaves in each image asset.


Click on the color box to change one of the colors in the palette. Use the slider, the mouse, and/or the RGB values to select a new shade.


Click out of the color select box, then give the custom palette a descriptive name, such as Colors.


Repeat this process for 3-4 colors in the palette, then click Apply. Be mindful that Player image assets will also be used in this project.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you pick an image from the Gallery that has a lot of solid colors that are easy to fill and modify?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Which image from the Gallery might you use to display an outdoor scene?

❓ What colors might you change to create 4 unique background image assets?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 As the ninja is selecting a background image from the Gallery, point out that it will be useful to pick an image that has a lot of solid colors that are easy to fill and modify. 

💡 After the ninja has selected their background image, have them consider which colors will be easiest to change in the image, as well as what colors they should replace them with to create a unique scene.
steps.instructions:
Customize a background image to create 4 unique assets to start the project!


Create a new image asset, then select one of the outdoor scene background images from the Gallery. 


Duplicate the background image asset 3 times, so that there are 4 background image assets total. In each new asset, use the fill tool to change the colors of the image so that each one represents one of the 4 seasons: Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter. Use the colors from the update color palette to differentiate the 4 images.


Rename the background image assets: springBackground, summerBackground, autumnBackground, and winterBackground.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add and name one image asset and 2 animation assets for a Player sprite to My Assets?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What sprite image and animation assets might be used for the Player sprite in this project?

❓ Why are both left and right-facing animation assets needed in the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Point out to the ninja that this is a 2D project, meaning that the user’s perspective is from the side (rather than top-down). Because of this, it’s important to match the sprite’s direction to the user’s controls. If the user presses the right direction button, the sprite animation asset should show the Player sprite moving right (and vice versa).
steps.instructions:
Create assets for a Player sprite.

 

Add 3 assets that will be used for a Player sprite: a still image, a right-facing animation asset, and a left-facing animation asset. Give each asset a descriptive name.


In the Gallery, notice that some of the colors for the sprite images may appear differently, based on the colors adjusted in the color palette. Revise the color palette as needed to update the sprite appearance.

steps.hints: ❓Did you type assets, a dot operator, and the asset type, followed by the name of the asset inside 2 backticks `` in the tilemap parameter?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What function should be used to display a tilemap on screen?

❓ Where should the name of the tilemap be typed in the setCurrentTilemap function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to check the documentation if they need help displaying a tilemap on screen.
steps.instructions:
Create a tilemap to display on the bottom of the screen.


Add a new tilemap asset that is 10 x 8, so that the tilemap is the size of the screen.


Create a path of tiles along the bottom of the screen. Give the tilemap asset a descriptive name. 


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add a // project initialization comment at the top. Display the tilemap asset underneath. 


Click ▶ to see the tilemap appear on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you type assets, a dot operator, the asset type and the asset name inside 2 backticks `` for each element in the backgroundList array?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Are the elements in the backgroundList array and the seasonList string array in the same order?

❓ What might the backgroundList image array and the seasonList string array be used for in this project? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure that the ninja has listed the elements in the backgroundList and seasonList arrays in the same order. In the project, the background image will display on the screen and the Player sprite will say the corresponding season name. It’s important that the elements are in the correct order so that the matching image and string appear together.
steps.instructions:
Store the customized assets in 2 arrays!


Below // project initialization, create a backgroundList array to store each of the 4 customized background image assets.


Create a seasonList string array to store the names of each season in the same order as the backgroundList array. 


Each matching background image and string should have the same index number in their respective arrays.

steps.hints: ❓Did you type the backgroundIndex variable inside the brackets of the backgroundList array to select the first background image from the array?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might the backgroundIndex variable control in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In this project, the backgroundIndex variable will control which image (and season) appear on the screen. Using a variable will allow each image asset and string to easily be cycled through on screen.

💡 Remind the ninja to use the documentation if they need help using a variable to access an index from an array.
steps.instructions:
Use an index variable to display the background image!


Below the arrays, declare a backgroundIndex variable set to 0.


Set the background image to the backgroundIndex of the backgroundList array.


Click ▶ to see the first background image from the array appear.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use 2 onEvent controller functions to change the scrolling direction?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the right direction button is pressed? What happens when the left direction button is pressed?

❓ Why should different vx arguments be used in the 2 onEvent controller functions?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Point out to the ninja that they can type in “scroll” at the top of the extensions search bar to easily find the scroller extension.

💡When the right direction button is pressed, the background will scroll to the left. When the left direction button is pressed, the background will scroll to the right. The vx parameter should be a negative value to cause the screen to move left and a positive value to cause the screen to move right.
steps.instructions:
Make the background scroll when the direction buttons are pressed!


Click Extensions, then select the arcade-background-scroll extension to add it to the project.


Add a // project events comment with button pressed events for both the right and left buttons underneath.


Open Scroller, then drag [scroll background with vx(-50) vy (-50)] into both button pressed events. 


Update the vx and vy parameters to -30, 0 for the right button, and 30, 0 for the left. 


Click ▶ to test the scrolling effect.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use 2 onEvent controller functions to stop the background scrolling?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the right direction button is released? What happens when the left direction button is released?

❓ Why should the same vx and vy arguments be used in the 2 onEvent controller functions? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the right or left direction buttons are released, the background will stop scrolling. Both vx and vy parameters should be set to 0 once the direction buttons are released, so that the user controls when the background scrolls and when it does not.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can delete .Pressed, retype the dot operator, then select Released, to change the code that triggers each onEvent function to run.
steps.instructions:
Stop the background from scrolling if the direction buttons are released!


Underneath the 2 button pressed events, add 2 on button released events set to right and left.


Open Scroller, drag scrollBackgroundWithSpeed inside each event. Set both the vx and vy parameters to 0. Now, the scrolling will stop whenever the direction buttons are released.


Click ▶ to test the scrolling effect.

steps.hints: ❓Did you cut and paste the code that sets the background image into the onUpdate loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Which background image appears when the project is run? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Because the backgroundIndex variable is still set to 0, the first image in the backgroundList array will appear on screen. This will change throughout the project to update what background image is displayed.
steps.instructions:
Use a loop to scroll through the 4 backgrounds!


Add an onUpdate loop under // project events. 


Cut the code that sets the background image from the backgroundList array and paste it inside the onUpdate loop.


Click ▶ to test that the correct background image appears.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an increment operator ++ to increase the backgroundIndex variable by 1?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the getBackgroundXOffset function return? Why might it be useful to use?

❓ When will the value of the backgroundIndex variable be increased by 1?

❓ What symbol might be used to increase the value of the backgroundIndex variable by 1? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The getBackgroundXOffset function returns the number of pixels that the background is offset by. It can be useful for identifying the offset between where a background image began and where it appears on the screen.

💡 If the right direction button is pressed AND the x-offset is less than 1, the backgroundIndex variable will be increased by 1, and will cycle to the next background image in the array.

💡 Remind the ninja that there are several ways to increase the value of a variable by 1. Prompt them to think about different symbols and values to use to achieve this (such as an increment operator ++ or an addition assignment operator +=).
steps.instructions:
Scroll the background to the right!


Above the setBackgroundImage function, add a conditional inside the onUpdate loop that checks if the right button is pressed. 


Type an AND operator, then open Scroller to drag [background offset x] inside the parentheses. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

scroller.getBackgroundXOffset()

The getBackgroundXOffset function returns the current x-offset of the scrolled background. This keeps track of how far left or right the background image has scrolled on the screen.


Check if the getBackgroundXOffset() is less than 1. Inside the conditional, increase the backgroundIndex variable by 1. 


Click ▶ to test the scrolling effect and notice the background change.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an equality operator == to check the value of the backgroundIndex variable in the nested if conditional?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the onUpdate loop runs?

❓ When will the backgroundIndex variable be reset to 0?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Previously when the onUpdate loop ran, it cycled through all of the background images by increasing the backgroundIndex variable by 1 each time a new image appeared. By adding an else condition, if the last element in the backgroundList array is displayed on screen, the first image in the array will be shown instead.
steps.instructions:
Oh no, the project ends after the final background image in the array!


Nest another conditional inside the existing conditional that checks if the backgroundIndex variable is equal to 3, then resets the variable to 0 if true.


Add an else condition, then cut and paste backgroundIndex++ inside. 


Now, the background image will reset to the first background image after all 4 images have been cycled through.


Click ▶ to test if the scrolling effect keeps cycling through all 4 background images in the array.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add a nested if conditional inside the else if conditional?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓What symbol might be used to decrease the backgroundIndex variable by 1?

❓ What symbol should be used to check if multiple conditions are true in the else if condition? 

❓ Why should the scene update if if the left direction button is pressed AND if the background x-offset value is greater than 159?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that there are several ways to decrease the value of a variable by 1. Prompt them to think about different symbols and values to use to achieve this (such as an decrement operator -- or a subtraction assignment operator -=). 

💡 Explain to the ninja that the getBackgroundXOffset function returns the number of pixels that the background is offset by. It can be useful for identifying the offset between where a background image began and where it appears on the screen.

💡Remind the ninja that an AND operator && should be used in the else if condition to check if the left direction button is pressed AND if the background x-offset value is greater than 159.
steps.instructions:
Scroll the background to the left!


In the onUpdate loop, add an else if condition that checks if the left button is pressed, and if the background x-offset value is greater than 159.

 

Add a conditional inside the else if  condition that checks if the backgroundIndex variable is 0, resetting it to 3 if true.


Add an else condition that will decrease the backgroundIndex variable by 1. 


Now, the background image will cycle through the opposite direction, and reset to the last image after all 4 images have been cycled through.


Click ▶ to test if the scrolling effect keeps cycling through all 4 background images using the right and left direction buttons.

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the x and y parameters of setBackgroundScrollOffset in each conditional?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓Why should the x and y parameters of the setBackgroundScrollOffset function be reset each time the background image changes?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The setBackgroundScrollOffset function will reset the background image scroll so that it won’t accidentally trigger the conditional to run more than once after one of the 2 conditions is met, which could result in one of the background images being “skipped” on screen.
steps.instructions:
Reset the background image position after it has changed.


Open Scroller, drag a [set background offset to x(0) y(0)] into the bottom of both nested conditionals. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

scroller.setBackgroundScrollOffset()

Update the x and y parameters to 159, 0 when the background is scrolling right, and to 1, 0 when the background is scrolling left.

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the tilemap coordinates so the Player sprite appears to be standing on top of a tilemap tile in the middle of the path?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓Where might the Player sprite be placed on the screen, so that it is on top of a tilemap tile?

❓Why should the background image be offset by 80 pixels when the project starts?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to use the documentation if they need help adding a sprite, setting the camera to follow it, or placing it on the tilemap.

💡 The background image should be offset by 80 pixels when the project starts so that it begins in the middle of the screen and the Player sprite will have to “move” the same distance left or right for the background image to change.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to walk through the scrolling backgrounds!


Under // project initialization, add a Player sprite and set it to the sprite image in My Assets. Set the camera to follow the Player sprite.


Place the Player sprite on top of a tilemap tile, in the middle of the screen. 


Open Scroller, drag [set background offset to x(0) y (0)] under the Player sprite code. Update the x and y parameters to 80, 0 so the Player sprite starts in the middle of the background scrolling effect.


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite in the project

steps.hints: ❓Did you update all 4 parameters in both runImageAnimation functions so that the sprite animations continuously loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What should the runImageAnimation function’s parameters be set to so that animation assets continuously loop when the right or left direction buttons are pressed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja to use the documentation for assistance updating the parameters of the runImageAnimation function. Encourage them to test out the animation to make sure it is running correctly.
steps.instructions:
Animate the Player sprite when it “walks” right or left.


Open Animation and drag runImageAnimation into both the right and left button pressed events. Update the parameters to make the Player sprite appear to walk right or left when the buttons are pressed, 


Click ▶ to test the Player sprite animation.

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the type and sprite parameters of the stopAnimation function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the stopAnimation function is run?

❓ Why should the Player sprite’s animation stop when the right and left buttons are released?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The stopAnimation function stops one type or all animations on a sprite. When the right and left buttons are released, the Player sprite should stop moving. As a result, the background stops scrolling and the sprite’s animation is stopped.
steps.instructions:
Stop the animation when the right and left buttons are released!


Open Animation and drag [stop (type) animations on (sprite)] into both right and left button released events. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


animation.stopAnimation(animation.

AnimationTypes.All, mySprite)


The stopAnimation function has 2 parameters: animation type and sprite. In the type parameter, replace .All with ImageAnimation then update the sprite parameter with the Player sprite name.


Click ▶ to test the Player sprite animation.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the seasonList array inside a sayText function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is it important to use the backgroundIndex variable when selecting from the both arrays?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that at the beginning of the project, the background images and season name string arrays stored the matching elements in the same order. As a result, the backgroundIndex variable can be used to access the same element in the array that matches the season shown in the background image.
steps.instructions:
Let the Player sprite announce the seasons as it “walks” through them!


Inside the onUpdate loop, code the sprite to say the names of each season as the background images change. Use the seasonList string array and the backgroundIndex variable to access the same element in the array that matches the season shown in the background image. 


Click ▶ to see the Player sprite announce the season it is walking through.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the setDialogTextColor to change the font color of the instructions?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What function and color might be used to change the text color in the dialog box?

❓ What images might be used for the dialog frame and cursor?


Sensei Pro Tip:


💡 Encourage the ninja to use the marquee tool in the editor to resize the cursor image.
steps.instructions:
Add instructions to the beginning of the project!


Before // project events, add a // project start comment. Underneath, set the dialog frame, cursor image, and/or the dialog text color.


Then, create a dialog box to share instructions for the project with the user.


Click ▶ to play the completed project!

subgroups.title: A Walk through the Seasons
subgroups.introduction: Modify background image assets from the gallery, and use the Scroller extension to create a project where a sprite “walks” through 4 scenes!

validationItems.text: Create a custom color palette in the Assets menu.
Customize 4 background image assets, then store the assets and their respective names in backgroundList and seasonList arrays.
Use a backgroundIndex variable to set the background image and have the Player sprite say the background name from their respective arrays.
Scroll the background image when the left and right direction buttons are pressed.
Stop the background image from scrolling when the left and right direction buttons are released.
Cycle through the background images when the left and right direction buttons are pressed.
Reset the background image position after it has changed.
Use 2 animation assets to animate the Player sprite when direction buttons are pressed, and stop when direction buttons are released.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 4 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about pixel art and how to use the asset editor to modify an existing asset. You will also use code from the Scroller and Images categories to enrich the project. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 4:

badges.title: Remixologist
badges.description: Use the paint editor to modify and remix existing pixel art image assets.

badges.title: Doppelganger
badges.description: Edit an existing asset to create multiple versions of the same image.

badges.title: Nice Change of Scenery
badges.description: Use the Scroller extension to create a background that scrolls and changes images as a sprite “walks”.

badges.title: Swatch and Learn
badges.description: Write code to get, set, and replace a pixel’s color on an image asset.

badges.title: A Refined Palette
badges.description: Use RGB values or hex color code to change the colors of the code editor’s color palette.

badges.title: Mixing it Up
badges.description: Use the Color Palette tool to change the default color palette with different colors.
